title: Complaints & Inspections Project (CIP): GCP & dbt Data Platform for Municipal Scale Infrastructure
text: To institutionalize a data-driven Complaints & Inspections Project (CIP), I architected an end-to-end ELT pipeline integrating high-volume NYC 311 service requests and Department of Health (DOHMH) cafeteria inspection records. By designing a Kimball-style star schema and deploying automated data ingestion via Google Cloud Platform, I transformed disjointed public datasets into a unified analytical data bus. This infrastructure empowers stakeholders to move from reactive troubleshooting to proactive operational monitoring, identifying critical systemic intersections to drive continuous service improvement

title: SDOH Project: Epidemiological Social Determinants of Health Analytics Engine
text:
Traditional public health models frequently default to using generic neighborhood poverty rates to explain health disparities, an approach that often hides more complex structural drivers. To test this limitation, our team architected a multi-layer analytical engine evaluating NYC HIV public health datasets (2019–2023) alongside localized Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) matrices across conformed ZIP code zones.
By implementing an offset Poisson regression model and unsupervised K-Means clustering, the engine successfully unmasked critical institutional anomalies—most notably the structural distortion caused by localized correctional populations—and demonstrated that wealth inequality (the Gini coefficient) serves as a far more potent predictor of localized health burden than income or poverty markers alone.

section: Phase 2: Predictive Engine & The Rikers Island Unmasking
text:
Phase 2: Predictive Engine & The Rikers Island Unmasking
Because HIV diagnosis records are count-based outcomes rather than continuous, un-bounded variables, ordinary multiple linear regression (MLR) models can output negative predictions and distort variance indicators. We deployed a Poisson generalized linear model (GLM) featuring a log-link function.
To properly scale the counts relative to varying neighborhood boundaries, we integrated 2020 Census population records directly into the model as an offset variable, effectively treating population scale as a fixed constant while modeling the underlying case distribution.

Engineering for Causal Anomalies (The Rikers Hack)
Initial diagnostic passes revealed an massive outlier footprint at ZIP code 11370—the geographical anchor for the Rikers Island correctional facility. Because an institutional population displays fundamentally different public health patterns than standard residential zones, this single data point introduced severe skewing across our multivariable correlation matrices.
To resolve this, we engineered an explicit institutional dummy variable directly into our final statistical sweep:

Deviance Optimization: Incorporating the institutional control variable caused the model’s baseline Deviance metric to drop from a highly unstable 27,695 down to an incredibly tight 3,644 in the sensitivity iteration.
Model Validation: The final sweep achieved a statistically robust McFadden’s Pseudo R-squared of 0.3922, confirming an elite fit for real-world categorical count modeling.
The Gini Indicator: The finalized model proved that the Gini coefficient (income inequality) maintained a powerful, independent positive relationship with elevated case counts, even when poverty and absolute household income metrics were held fully constant.

section: Phase 3: Unsupervised Machine Learning Profile Clustering
text:
Phase 3: Unsupervised Machine Learning Profile Clustering
To classify the 141 conformed ZIP codes based on overlapping layers of health metrics and socioeconomic context, we deployed an unsupervised K-Means clustering sequence, processing 14 continuous input features simultaneously.

Calibration & Cross-Method Validation
We tested cluster counts ranging from \(k = 2\) through \(k = 10\), evaluating them using a combined Elbow and Silhouette framework. While a simple \(k=2\) sequence offered the cleanest raw mathematical partition, we chose a 4-cluster solution to provide meaningful operational segments for real-world public health resource allocation:

title: WHO Project: Warm Hand-Off Transit-Accessible Provider Routing
text:
The WHO (Warm Hand-Off) Project originated from the front lines of crisis intervention and behavioral health (BH) triage. Designed to replace static, manually compiled referral lists, this tool integrates Federal and New York State Medicare/Medicaid provider networks with New York City Mass Transit Authority (MTA) infrastructure. It transforms a high-friction referral process into a dynamic, geospatial routing engine, ensuring patients transitioning to external care can locate active providers based on precise insurance alignment and accessible transit routes.
This tool is strictly scoped as a decision-support application for internal Care Coordinators and Social Workers, specifically targeting workflows like those used by Callen-Lorde’s BHART team.

text:
Architecture Pivot: From Data Warehouse to Serverless Web App
Initial scoping for this project centered on a traditional OLAP Data Warehouse model utilizing BigQuery and dbt. However, after consulting with CIS faculty and evaluating the latency needs of front-line clinical teams, the project scope was successfully pivoted to a serverless OLTP Web Application model.
This lightweight, serverless infrastructure optimizes for real-time, low-friction application performance (single-row lookups) rather than long-term historical analytics.

Technical Stack

Infrastructure: AWS S3, AWS Lambda
Data Bus & Processing: Python, Pandas

title: WHO Project: Warm Hand-Off Transit-Accessible Provider Routing
text:
The Implementation Workflow

1. The Python Data Bus
Instead of relying on a warehouse, a Python-driven data bus handles all API ingestion, geospatial calculations, and data normalization locally. It flattens the relational data into a singular, highly denormalized JSON dataset optimized for fast frontend reading.


2. Flat-File Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCDs)
Historical provider mobility is handled programmatically in the Python bus prior to AWS upload. An is_active flag retains historical footprints, preventing data decay from public portals while allowing the frontend map to instantly filter for current clinics.


3. Front-End Deep Linking & Privacy Governance
A major challenge in behavioral health routing is identifying micro-specialties and intersectional competencies not captured by state APIs. Rather than scraping proprietary directories, which introduces AWS Lambda timeout risks and clinical liability, the application utilizes dynamic UI Smart-Links.
The front-end natively constructs search URLs using available Socrata data and passes these parameters directly into external queries. This gives Care Coordinators a one-click workflow to visually verify therapeutic modalities while maintaining zero backend compute cost.

title: PEX Project: Patient Experience Survey Clustering
text:
The PEX Project is a statistical NLP and data mining initiative designed to transform unstructured patient feedback into actionable operational insights. Developed in collaboration with Patient Experience leadership, this tool utilizes text analytics and KMeans clustering to automatically categorize open-ended survey comments into interpretable service themes, such as communication, access, wait time, and staff courtesy.


Patient experience teams regularly receive a high volume of free-text comments[cite: 18]. Relying on manual review or basic keyword tallying (e.g., “Ctrl+F” searching) is highly inefficient, difficult to scale, and restricts analysis to preconceived terms. Consequently, valuable operational feedback is often buried in the sheer volume of unstructured data, delaying the team’s ability to identify and address recurring systemic issues.



This project establishes an automated, repeatable workflow that transcends basic text searching. By passing cleaned survey text through a TF-IDF vectorizer and grouping it via KMeans clustering, the tool dynamically discovers recurring themes. This allows stakeholders to rapidly move from reading raw volume to making data-supported operational decisions.

title: PEX Project: Patient Experience Survey Clustering
section: Methodology: Unsupervised Discovery vs. Predefined Categories
text:
Methodology: Unsupervised Discovery vs. Predefined Categories
This pipeline utilizes unsupervised machine learning. The algorithm is not trained on preconceived labels and does not inherently know what “Wait Time” or “Staff Courtesy” means. It strictly groups comments based on mathematical similarities and proximity in the vocabulary used.

The Algorithm’s Role: To do the heavy lifting. It objectively sorts thousands of unstructured comments into k distinct, mathematically related clusters.
The Human’s Role: To apply business context. The stakeholder reviews the top representative keywords for each generated cluster and assigns the appropriate operational label.

This dynamic approach ensures that themes emerge naturally from the patients’ actual words. Furthermore, by using a fixed mathematical seed during test set processing, the cluster boundaries are 100% reproducible every time the script is run by the analytics team.
